nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree that is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and let $k$ be a key (a pair of an integer low endpoint and a natural-number identifier). The tree $T'$ returned by keyed deletion of $k$ from $T$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is ignored) is again AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and the height of $T'$ is either the height of $T$ or one less.
nodes.title: Keyed deletion preserves AVL balance in an interval tree

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree that is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and let $e$ be an entry. The tree $T'$ returned by keyed insertion of $e$ into $T$ (which replaces an entry with the same key, if there is one; we take the tree component of the result and ignore the cost) is again AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and the height of $T'$ is either the height of $T$ or one more.
nodes.title: Keyed insertion preserves AVL balance in an interval tree

nodes.summary: Let $L$ and $R$ be interval trees that are AVL balanced with exact stored heights, with heights $h_L$ and $h_R$ satisfying $h_L \le h_R + 2$ and $h_R \le h_L + 2$, and let $e$ be an entry. Let $B$ be the tree obtained by rebalancing the node that the smart constructor builds from $L$, $e$ and $R$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is ignored). Then $B$ is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, the height…
nodes.title: Rebalancing a rebuilt interval-tree node restores AVL balance

nodes.summary: Let $L$ and $R$ be interval trees that are AVL balanced with exact stored heights, with heights $h_L$ and $h_R$ satisfying $h_L \le h_R + 2$ and $h_R \le h_L + 2$. Let $N$ be a node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ whose stored height is $\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$ (its stored size and stored maximum are arbitrary), and let $B$ be the tree obtained by rebalancing $N$ (the tree component of the…
nodes.title: Rebalancing an interval-tree node with exact stored height restores AVL balance

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree that is AVL balanced with exact stored heights. If removing the leftmost entry of $T$ succeeds and returns an entry $m$, a remaining tree $R$ and a cost $c$, then $R$ is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and the height of $R$ is either the height of $T$ or one less.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum preserves AVL balance in an interval tree

nodes.summary: An interval tree is AVL balanced with exact stored heights when it is empty, or when it is a node such that, writing $h_L$ and $h_R$ for the stored heights of its left and right subtrees (the empty tree has height $0$), the node's stored height equals $\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$, $h_L \le h_R + 1$, $h_R \le h_L + 1$, and both subtrees are again AVL balanced with exact stored heights.
nodes.title: AVL balance of an interval tree

nodes.summary: The balance check returns true on the empty tree. On a node whose left and right subtrees have stored heights $h_L$ and $h_R$ (the empty tree has height $0$), it returns true exactly when the node's stored height equals $\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$, $h_L \le h_R + 1$, $h_R \le h_L + 1$, and the check returns true on both subtrees.
nodes.title: Boolean AVL balance check for interval trees

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree satisfying the cache invariant (every cached maximum high endpoint, height and size is exact), and let $k$ be a key (a pair of an integer low endpoint and a natural-number identifier). The tree returned by keyed deletion of $k$ from $T$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is ignored) also satisfies the cache invariant. This includes keys that do not occur in $T$.
nodes.title: Keyed deletion preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree satisfying the cache invariant (every cached maximum high endpoint, height and size is exact), and let $e$ be an entry. The tree returned by keyed insertion of $e$ into $T$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is ignored) also satisfies the cache invariant. This includes the case where an entry with the same key is replaced.
nodes.title: Keyed insertion preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: If interval trees $L$ and $R$ satisfy the cache invariant (every cached maximum high endpoint, height and size is exact), then for every entry $e$ the node that the smart constructor builds from $L$, $e$ and $R$ also satisfies the cache invariant.
nodes.title: The interval-tree smart constructor preserves the cache invariant

nodes.summary: If the executable cache check returns true on an interval tree $t$, then $t$ satisfies the cache invariant.
nodes.title: The executable cache check implies the cache invariant

nodes.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then the tree returned by the rebalancing step at the root of $t$ also satisfies the cache invariant.
nodes.title: Rebalancing preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be an interval tree that satisfies the cache invariant. If removing the leftmost entry of $t$ succeeds and returns an entry, a tree $t'$ and an operation cost, then $t'$ satisfies the cache invariant.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the left-right double rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged unless $t$ has a nonempty left subtree whose right subtree is nonempty.
nodes.title: Left-right rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the left rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged when $t$ is empty or has an empty right subtree.
nodes.title: Left rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the right-left double rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged unless $t$ has a nonempty right subtree whose left subtree is nonempty.
nodes.title: Right-left rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the right rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged when $t$ is empty or has an empty left subtree.
nodes.title: Right rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant

nodes.summary: An interval tree satisfies the cache invariant when every cached field is exact, recursively. The empty tree satisfies it. A node with stored height $h$, stored size $s$, stored maximum $m$, left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ satisfies it when $L$ and $R$ satisfy it, $m$ is at least the high endpoint of every entry of $L$, of $e$ and of every entry of $R$, $m$ equals the high endpoint of one of these…
nodes.title: Cache invariant of an interval tree

nodes.summary: The Boolean cache check returns true on the empty tree. On a node with stored height $h$, stored size $s$, stored maximum $m$, left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ it returns true exactly when $h = \max(\operatorname{height} L, \operatorname{height} R) + 1$, $s = \operatorname{size} L + \operatorname{size} R + 1$, $m$ is the largest of the high endpoint of $e$ and the cached maxima of those of $L$ and…
nodes.title: Executable cache check for interval trees

nodes.summary: The cached maximum of an interval tree is no value when the tree is empty, and when the tree is a node it is the integer stored in the node's cached maximum-high-endpoint field.
nodes.title: Cached maximum of an interval tree

nodes.summary: For an indexed interval tree, the check returns true exactly when all of the following hold: at every node the cached height and size agree with the values recomputed from its children's cached heights and sizes, and the cached maximum high endpoint equals the largest of the node's own high endpoint and its children's cached maxima; the tree is AVL-balanced (sibling heights differ by at most one) with exact stored…
nodes.title: Representation check for the indexed interval tree

nodes.summary: For keys $(a, i)$ and $(b, j)$ in $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ (a low endpoint and an occurrence identifier), the comparison returns less-than if $a < b$, or if $a = b$ and $i < j$; greater-than if $a > b$, or if $a = b$ and $i > j$; and equal if $a = b$ and $i = j$.
nodes.title: Lexicographic comparison of keys

nodes.summary: A cost record for the interval tree consists of seven natural-number counters, each defaulting to $0$: node visits, key comparisons, endpoint comparisons, cached-maximum reads, cache writes, rotations, and identifier-index operations.
nodes.title: Operation cost counters for interval trees

nodes.summary: An entry of the interval tree consists of an identifier, which is a natural number, and an interval with integer low and high endpoints.
nodes.title: Interval tree entry

nodes.summary: The key of an entry is the pair $(\ell, i) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ of its low endpoint $\ell$ and identifier $i$; keys are compared lexicographically. Let $T$ be an interval tree whose keys are strictly ordered (every key in a left subtree is lexicographically below its node's key and every key in a right subtree is above it), and let $k \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ be a key. Then the in-order list…
nodes.title: Keyed erasure removes exactly the entries with that key

nodes.summary: Erasing a key $k \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ from an interval tree returns a new tree together with its cost; the key of an entry is the pair of its low endpoint and identifier, and keys are compared lexicographically. The empty tree is returned unchanged at a cost of one node visit. At a node with entry $x$, the key $k$ is compared with the key of $x$. If $k$ is smaller, $k$ is erased from the left subtree;…
nodes.title: Keyed erasure with cost

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree satisfying the representation invariant, and let $i$ be a natural number. Then the tree obtained by erasing identifier $i$ from $T$ again satisfies the invariant, and an entry is stored in it if and only if it is stored in $T$ and its identifier differs from $i$.
nodes.title: Correctness of erasure from the indexed interval tree

nodes.summary: To erase identifier $i$ from an indexed interval tree, look $i$ up in the identifier index. If it is absent, the tree is returned unchanged at a cost of one index operation. If the index maps $i$ to a low endpoint $\ell$, the entry with key $(\ell, i)$ is erased from the underlying interval tree, $i$ is removed from the index, and the cost is the cost of the keyed erasure plus two index operations.
nodes.title: Erasure by identifier with cost

nodes.summary: For an indexed interval tree, the backward index check returns true exactly when, for every identifier $i$ that the identifier index maps to a low endpoint $\ell$, some stored entry has identifier $i$ and an interval with low endpoint $\ell$.
nodes.title: Backward identifier-index check

nodes.summary: For an indexed interval tree, the forward index check returns true exactly when the identifier index maps the identifier of every stored entry to the low endpoint of that entry's interval.
nodes.title: Forward identifier-index check

nodes.summary: An indexed interval tree consists of a root interval tree together with an identifier index: a finite map, implemented as a balanced search tree, from natural-number identifiers to integer low endpoints.
nodes.title: Indexed interval tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a tree whose entries are strictly ordered by key, and let $x$ be an entry. The in-order list of entries of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ by key is a permutation of the list consisting of $x$ followed by those entries of $t$ whose key differs from the key of $x$.
nodes.title: Entries after keyed insertion

nodes.summary: Inserting an entry $x$ into a tree returns a new tree together with an operation cost; keys (low endpoint, then identifier) are compared lexicographically. Into the empty tree, $x$ is inserted as a single node, at a cost of one node visit and one cache write. At a node with entry $y$: if the key of $x$ equals the key of $y$, then $y$ is replaced by $x$, at a cost of one node visit, one key comparison and one cache…
nodes.title: Keyed insertion with cost

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree satisfying the representation invariant, and let $x$ be an entry whose interval is valid (its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint). If inserting $x$ into $T$ succeeds with result $T'$, then $T'$ satisfies the representation invariant, $x$ is stored in the root tree of $T'$, and an entry $e$ is stored in the root tree of $T'$ if and only if either $e = x$, or $e$ is stored…
nodes.title: Correctness of insertion into an indexed interval tree

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree and let $e$ be an entry with identifier $i$ and interval $[a, b]$. Inserting $e$ into $T$ first tests $a \le b$. If $a > b$, it returns no tree, at a cost of one endpoint comparison. Otherwise, if the identifier index of $T$ maps $i$ to a low endpoint $\ell$, the entry with key $(\ell, i)$ is erased from the root tree of $T$ by keyed erasure; if $i$ is not in the index, the root…
nodes.title: Insertion by identifier with cost

nodes.summary: An interval is a pair of integers, its low endpoint and its high endpoint, read as the closed interval from the low to the high endpoint. The structure itself imposes no order on the endpoints; the public update operations accept an interval only when its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint.
nodes.title: Interval

nodes.summary: If the executable checker returns true on an indexed interval tree $T$, then $T$ satisfies the representation invariant.
nodes.title: Soundness of the invariant checker

nodes.summary: An indexed interval tree $T$ satisfies the representation invariant when its root tree has exact cached metadata (heights, sizes, and attained maximum high endpoints), is strictly ordered by the composite key (low endpoint, then identifier), is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and stores only valid intervals; the identifiers of the stored entries are pairwise distinct; the identifier index maps the…
nodes.title: Representation invariant of an indexed interval tree

nodes.summary: Given an optional lower bound, an optional upper bound and a key $k$ (a pair of an integer and a natural number), this test returns true exactly when the lower bound is absent or strictly below $k$, and the upper bound is absent or strictly above $k$. Keys are compared lexicographically: first by the integer, then by the natural number.
nodes.title: Key between optional bounds

nodes.summary: If a tree is strictly ordered by key, then the keys of its stored entries are pairwise distinct.
nodes.title: Strictly key-ordered trees have distinct keys

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a key-ordered interval tree and let $k \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ be a key. Then the tree returned by the cost-instrumented keyed deletion of $k$ from $t$ (the reported cost is discarded) is again key-ordered.
nodes.title: Deletion from an interval tree preserves key ordering

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a key-ordered interval tree and let $e$ be an entry. Then the tree returned by the cost-instrumented keyed insertion of $e$ into $t$ (which replaces the entry with the same key, if there is one; the reported cost is discarded) is again key-ordered.
nodes.title: Insertion into an interval tree preserves key ordering

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be an interval tree and let $\ell$ and $u$ be optional keys in $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$. If the executable ordering check of $t$ with lower bound $\ell$ and upper bound $u$ succeeds, then $t$ is key-ordered, and every entry $e$ stored in $t$ satisfies $\ell < \operatorname{key}(e)$ when $\ell$ is present and $\operatorname{key}(e) < u$ when $u$ is present, where $<$ is the lexicographic order on keys…
nodes.title: The executable ordering check implies key ordering

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a key-ordered interval tree. If the cost-instrumented removal of the leftmost entry of $t$ succeeds, returning that entry, a remaining tree $t'$ and a cost, then $t'$ is key-ordered.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum from an interval tree preserves key ordering

nodes.summary: The empty tree is key-ordered, and a node is key-ordered when both of its subtrees are key-ordered, the key of every entry in the left subtree is strictly less than the key of the node's entry, and the key of the node's entry is strictly less than the key of every entry in the right subtree. Keys are compared lexicographically: low endpoint first, then identifier.
nodes.title: Key-ordered interval tree

nodes.summary: The key of an entry is the pair $(\ell, i) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$, where $\ell$ is the low endpoint of the entry's interval and $i$ is the entry's identifier.
nodes.title: Search key of an interval entry

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be an interval tree and let $\ell$ and $u$ be optional keys in $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$. If the executable ordering check of $t$ with lower bound $\ell$ and upper bound $u$ succeeds, then $t$ is low-endpoint ordered, and every entry $e$ stored in $t$ satisfies $\ell < \operatorname{key}(e)$ when $\ell$ is present and $\operatorname{key}(e) < u$ when $u$ is present, where $<$ is the lexicographic order…
nodes.title: The executable ordering check implies low-endpoint ordering

nodes.summary: The empty tree is low-endpoint ordered, and a node is low-endpoint ordered when both of its subtrees are low-endpoint ordered, every interval in the left subtree has low endpoint at most the low endpoint of the node's interval, and the node's low endpoint is at most the low endpoint of every interval in the right subtree.
nodes.title: Low-endpoint ordered interval tree

nodes.summary: For an integer $a$ and an optional integer $v$, the value is $a$ when $v$ is absent and $\max(a, v)$ when $v$ is present. It combines a value with an optional subtree maximum without using a sentinel value.
nodes.title: Maximum with an optional value

nodes.summary: For an interval tree $T$ write $h(T)$ and $|T|$ for its cached height and size, both $0$ for the empty tree. Given interval trees $L$ and $R$ and an entry $e$, this builds the node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ whose cached height is $\max(h(L), h(R)) + 1$, whose cached size is $|L| + |R| + 1$, and whose cached maximum high endpoint is the largest of the high endpoint of $e$ and the cached…
nodes.title: Node construction with repaired metadata

nodes.summary: For subtrees $L$ and $R$ and an entry $e$, the node maximum is the largest of the high endpoint of the interval of $e$, the cached maximum high endpoint stored at the root of $L$, and the one stored at the root of $R$, where an empty subtree stores no cached maximum and contributes nothing.
nodes.title: Maximum high endpoint at a node

nodes.summary: For a tree $T$ and a query interval $q$, the oracle search returns the first entry, in the in-order list of entries of $T$, whose interval overlaps $q$ as closed intervals, and returns nothing when no entry's interval overlaps $q$.
nodes.title: Linear-scan overlap search

nodes.summary: Keys of entries are pairs (low endpoint, identifier), ordered lexicographically. Given optional lower and upper key bounds $\ell$ and $u$, the check accepts the empty tree, and accepts a node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when the key $k$ of $e$ is strictly greater than $\ell$ if $\ell$ is present and strictly less than $u$ if $u$ is present, the interval of $e$ has low endpoint at…
nodes.title: Ordered-and-valid check for interval trees

nodes.summary: For an interval $I$ with low endpoint $a$ and high endpoint $b$ and an interval $J$ with low endpoint $c$ and high endpoint $d$, the overlap test of $I$ against $J$ returns true exactly when $a \le d$ and $c \le b$; it compares $a$ with $d$ first and returns false without the second comparison when $a > d$.
nodes.title: Overlap test for closed intervals

nodes.summary: For intervals $I$ and $J$, the Boolean component of the instrumented overlap test of $I$ against $J$ equals the overlap test of $I$ against $J$.
nodes.title: The instrumented overlap test returns the plain result

nodes.summary: For intervals $I$ and $J$, the instrumented overlap test of $I$ against $J$ reports $2$ endpoint comparisons when the low endpoint of $I$ is at most the high endpoint of $J$, and $1$ comparison otherwise.
nodes.title: Comparison count of the overlap test

nodes.summary: For an interval $I$ with low endpoint $a$ and high endpoint $b$ and an interval $J$ with low endpoint $c$ and high endpoint $d$, the instrumented overlap test of $I$ against $J$ returns the pair (false, $1$) when $a > d$, the pair (false, $2$) when $a \le d$ and $c > b$, and the pair (true, $2$) when $a \le d$ and $c \le b$; the number is the count of endpoint comparisons evaluated.
nodes.title: Overlap test with comparison count

nodes.summary: An interval $I$ with low endpoint $a$ and high endpoint $b$ overlaps an interval $J$ with low endpoint $c$ and high endpoint $d$ when $a \le d$ and $c \le b$; in particular, intervals that share only an endpoint overlap.
nodes.title: Overlapping closed intervals

nodes.summary: Rebalancing a tree $T$ returns a tree and a cost, where heights are the stored heights. If $T$ is empty, or neither subtree of its root is more than one taller than the other, it returns $T$ unchanged with zero cost. If the left subtree $L$ is more than one taller than the right subtree, it applies a right rotation, costing $2$ cache writes and one rotation, when the left child of $L$ is at least as tall as the…
nodes.title: AVL rebalancing step with cost

nodes.summary: If removing the leftmost entry of a tree $T$ returns an entry $m$, a tree $T'$ and a cost, then the list consisting of $m$ followed by the in-order entries of $T'$ is a permutation of the in-order entries of $T$.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum preserves the other entries

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a key-ordered interval tree: at every node, the keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller and those in the right subtree strictly larger than the node's key, where the key of an entry is the pair (low endpoint, identifier) compared lexicographically. If removing the leftmost entry of $T$ returns the entry $m$ (together with the remaining tree and a cost record), then every entry $e$ stored in $T$ is…
nodes.title: The removed minimum has the least key

nodes.summary: Removing the leftmost entry of an interval tree $T$ returns nothing when $T$ is empty. When the root's left subtree is empty, it returns the root entry, the right subtree, and a cost of one node visit. Otherwise it removes the leftmost entry $m$ of the left subtree recursively (returning nothing if that fails), rebuilds the root node over the new left subtree with recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint,…
nodes.title: Removing the leftmost entry, with its cost

nodes.summary: Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The left-right rotation sends $\langle\langle a, x, \langle b, y, c\rangle\rangle, z, d\rangle$ to $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, \langle c, z, d\rangle\rangle$, where all three nodes of the result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned unchanged.
nodes.title: Left-right double rotation

nodes.summary: Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The left rotation sends $\langle a, x, \langle b, y, c\rangle\rangle$ to $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, c\rangle$, where both nodes of the result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned unchanged.
nodes.title: Left rotation

nodes.summary: Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The right-left rotation sends $\langle a, x, \langle\langle b, y, c\rangle, z, d\rangle\rangle$ to $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, \langle c, z, d\rangle\rangle$, where all three nodes of the result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned unchanged.
nodes.title: Right-left double rotation

nodes.summary: Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The right rotation sends $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, c\rangle$ to $\langle a, x, \langle b, y, c\rangle\rangle$, where both nodes of the result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned unchanged.
nodes.title: Right rotation

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree satisfying its representation invariant, and let $Q$ be a valid query interval (low endpoint at most high endpoint). If some entry stored in $T$ has an interval that overlaps $Q$ (each interval's low endpoint is at most the other's high endpoint), then searching $T$ for $Q$ returns some entry.
nodes.title: Completeness of indexed interval search

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree whose cached height, size and maximum high endpoint are exact at every node, and whose low endpoints respect the search order (at every node, low endpoints in the left subtree are at most the node's, and those in the right subtree at least the node's). If some entry stored in $T$ has an interval that overlaps the query interval $Q$ (each interval's low endpoint is at most the other's…
nodes.title: Completeness of interval-tree search

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree whose cached height, size and maximum high endpoint are exact at every node, and whose low endpoints respect the search order (at every node, low endpoints in the left subtree are at most the node's, and those in the right subtree at least the node's). Then searching $T$ for a query interval $Q$ returns nothing if and only if no entry stored in $T$ has an interval that overlaps $Q$ (each…
nodes.title: Interval-tree search fails exactly when nothing overlaps

nodes.summary: The search of an indexed interval tree $T$ for a query interval $q = [c, d]$ returns nothing when $c > d$, and otherwise returns the entry, if any, found by the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in the root tree of $T$. For every indexed interval tree $T$, every query interval $q$ and every entry $e$, if this search returns $e$, then $e$ is one of the entries stored in the root tree of $T$ and the interval of $e$…
nodes.title: Soundness of indexed interval-tree search

nodes.summary: For every query interval $q$, the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in the empty interval tree returns no entry, and its cost record counts one node visit and zero for every other counter (key comparisons, endpoint comparisons, cached-maximum reads, cache writes, rotations and index operations).
nodes.title: Instrumented search in the empty tree

nodes.summary: Let $e$ be an entry whose interval is $[a, b]$, let $q = [c, d]$ be a query interval, and let $k = 2$ if $a \le d$ and $k = 1$ otherwise. Consider the single-node tree built from $e$ with empty subtrees and exact cached fields. If $[a, b]$ and $[c, d]$ overlap (that is, $a \le d$ and $c \le b$), the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in this tree returns $e$ with a cost record of one node visit and $k$ endpoint…
nodes.title: Instrumented search in a one-entry tree

nodes.summary: Given a query interval $q = [c, d]$ and an interval tree $T$, the instrumented overlap search returns an optional entry together with a cost record, defined by recursion on $T$. On the empty tree it returns no entry and records one node visit. At a node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ with interval $[a, b]$ and right subtree $R$, it first tests overlap by evaluating $a \le d$ and, only if that holds, $c \le b$;…
nodes.title: Instrumented overlap search

nodes.summary: The overlap search of a query interval $q$ in an interval tree $T$ returns the optional entry produced by the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in $T$, discarding its cost record.
nodes.title: Interval-tree overlap search

nodes.summary: An interval tree is either empty or a node consisting of a left subtree, an entry, a right subtree and three cached fields: a height and a size (natural numbers) and a maximum high endpoint (an integer). The type imposes no balance or consistency condition on these fields; it is the carrier on which the AVL interval-tree operations act.
nodes.title: Interval tree

nodes.summary: For an interval $[a, b]$ with integer endpoints, the Boolean validity test returns true exactly when $a \le b$.
nodes.title: Boolean interval validity test

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree in which every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$. Then for every key $(\ell, i)$ with $\ell$ an integer and $i$ a natural number, the tree returned by keyed erasure of $(\ell, i)$ from $T$ also has every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfying $a \le b$.
nodes.title: Keyed erasure preserves interval validity

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree in which every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$, and let $e$ be an entry whose interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$. Then the tree returned by keyed insertion of $e$ into $T$ also has every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfying $a \le b$.
nodes.title: Keyed insertion preserves interval validity

nodes.summary: If an interval tree $T$ satisfies the validity invariant, then every entry stored in $T$ has an interval $[a, b]$ with $a \le b$.
nodes.title: Stored intervals of a valid tree are valid

nodes.summary: If $L$ and $R$ are interval trees satisfying the validity invariant and $e$ is an entry whose interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$, then the node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$, built by the node constructor that recomputes the cached fields, satisfies the validity invariant.
nodes.title: Node construction preserves interval validity

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree and let $\ell$ and $u$ be optional lower and upper key bounds. If the executable check of $T$ with bounds $\ell$ and $u$, which tests that every key lies strictly between its bounds and that every stored interval passes the Boolean validity test, returns true, then every interval stored in $T$ is valid, that is, its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint.
nodes.title: The ordering check implies interval validity

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree in which every stored interval is valid (its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint). If the instrumented removal of the leftmost entry of $T$ succeeds, returning that entry $m$, the remaining tree $T'$ and a cost record $c$, then every interval stored in $T'$ is valid.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum preserves interval validity

nodes.summary: A tree satisfies the validity invariant when every interval stored in it is valid, that is, its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint. Recursively, the empty tree satisfies it, and a node satisfies it when its left subtree does, the interval of its entry is valid, and its right subtree does.
nodes.title: Validity invariant of an interval tree

nodes.summary: A closed interval with integer endpoints $a$ (low) and $b$ (high) is valid when its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint, $a \le b$.
nodes.title: Valid interval

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
